sections.overview: The white stork is a large wading bird that breeds across Europe, North Africa and western Asia, then winters in Africa or nearer regions.
sections.identification: Adults are about 95–110 cm long, 100–125 cm tall, span 155–200 cm and weigh 2.3–4.5 kg. Males average slightly larger, but the sexes share the same plumage. The source reports species ranges rather than a separate male/female mass table. Newly hatched young have dark bills and dull yellow-grey legs, which turn red as they mature.
sections.habitat: The species favours open landscapes where it can see and reach prey: floodplains, marsh edges, wet meadows, pastures and cultivated fields. In Alsace, Rhine-valley ried meadows are characteristic; across its range, nests also stand on trees, roofs, chimneys and purpose-built platforms.
sections.diet: As it walks, the stork spots prey, snaps it up in a bill thrust and regurgitates food for chicks. Its menu is opportunistic rather than frog-centred: earthworms, insects, small mammals, amphibians, reptiles and fish all feature. In dry conditions insects and mice may dominate, whereas wetter seasons make aquatic prey more available. A Polish study found that grassland and uncultivated margins supplied much of the food, alongside prey from fields and wetlands.
sections.behavior: Adults are quiet compared with many birds: they greet a mate or warn rivals with loud bill-clattering, raising and lowering the head and neck. Pairs also use postures and wing movements during courtship and nest defence. On migration, the stork saves energy by circling in rising columns of warm air called thermals, then gliding as the air carries it forward. Because thermals weaken over open sea, European birds funnel around the Mediterranean through the Strait of Gibraltar or the Bosporus rather than crossing directly. Migration differs among individuals and regions: many western and central European birds travel to Africa, while some winter in Iberia or southern France and some remain near reliable food. Landfills have helped sustain resident groups in Iberia, changing local movements without making every population sedentary.
sections.reproduction: Pairs reuse and enlarge bulky nests of sticks, often on high structures; the female usually lays three to five eggs, incubated by both adults for about a month. Incubation starts before the clutch is complete, so chicks hatch asynchronously; both parents feed them, and the young begin flying at about eight to ten weeks.
sections.ecology: Storks consume insects such as grasshoppers, which farmers may regard as pests, as well as rodents and other prey. Eagles and other large raptors may prey on young storks. GPS tracking in Spain and Morocco shows birds moving from landfills to wetlands and rice fields, linking separate habitats. These journeys create a possible route for litter or contaminants to move between waste sites and wetlands in droppings or regurgitated pellets.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment, published in 2025 after assessment on 5 June 2025, lists the species as Least Concern and increasing, with an estimated 526,000–588,000 mature birds. This is a global risk category, not a claim that every regional population is secure. In Alsace, numbers fell from about 145 breeding pairs in 1960 to only nine in 1974, amid deaths during migration and on African wintering grounds, as well as drought and habitat pressures. From the early 1970s, local groups held storks in enclosures for three years before release, encouraging them to settle and breed locally; later nest platforms and habitat work helped the population expand. Current hazards include wetland loss, intensive land management, electrocution and collisions with overhead wires, as well as hunting along some migration routes. A newer localized concern is landfill feeding: litter may be ingested, and movements between waste sites and wetlands create a possible transfer route.
